title: Debt and ease
hookLine: pay debts, and be easy on debtors (2:280)
tomorrow: groceries for your own family: a chore, or charity?

cards: An index card taped beside a register, a name at the top and a column of numbers in pencil. A folded IOU in a kitchen drawer, gone soft from being opened. The small scratch of a pen when a line gets crossed out.

Somebody owes, and they can't pay. Now what? The Qur'an answers in two steps, in Pickthall's words: "And if the debtor is in straitened circumstances, then (let there be) postponement to (the time of) ease".

teach.b: Step one is time. If the debtor is struggling, you wait until things ease.

teach.h: STEP TWO: LET IT GO, AS CHARITY.
teach.b: Step two comes in the same verse: to let the debt go, as charity, as sadaqah, is better for you, if you only knew. Wait first, and then, if you can, cross the line out.

A report in Sahih al-Bukhari tells of a merchant who lent to people and told his servant: when you come to someone in hardship, overlook it, so that perhaps God will overlook us. And the Prophet ﷺ said God overlooked him.
The ease he gave came back to him. But the verse isn't a loophole for the one who owes.
The same collection has the Prophet calling delay by someone who is able to pay an injustice. So there are two hands in every debt.
The borrower's: pay when you can, and don't stall. The lender's: when they truly can't, give them room, and maybe give them the whole of it.
One to tell a friend: in that report, a merchant's whole record came down to how he treated people who couldn't pay.

how: Muslims are taught to repay debts promptly when able, to write debts down, and, as lenders, to give a struggling borrower more time or forgive the debt as charity.

o: charging a fee to anyone who pays back late
borrowing freely, since all money owed is forgiven
paying what you owe, and easing those who owe you

games.q: the two hands of a debt — tap the pairs.
p: wait until a time of ease

s: the Qur'an tells lenders to give a struggling debtor time
2:280: postponement to the time of ease, and letting it go as charity is better.
forgiving a debt is simply losing money
the verse counts it as charity, and says it is better for you.
ease for the debtor means the borrower needn't hurry
the Prophet called delay by someone able to pay an injustice.

games.q: you owe a friend for concert tickets. you just got paid, and she said 'no rush'. you'd like to spend it on something else first. what fits?
o: she said no rush, so the other thing comes first.
pay her now: delaying when you're able to pay is a wrong.
pay half now and the rest whenever it's easy.
games.why: the ease in 2:280 is for the debtor who can't pay. for someone who can, the Prophet called delay an injustice.

practice: Hold a coin, or any small thing, in your open palm and feel its weight. Bring to mind one debt, one you owe or one owed to you by someone who's struggling.
Close your hand around it for a debt you'll pay; leave it open and flat for one you might ease. Stay with the weight for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Debt and ease: pay what you owe when you're able, and give the struggling debtor time, or let it go as charity.

orig.note: Arabic: a debt, something owed to another.

carryVoice: Something to keep: ease for the debtor, time first, and maybe the whole of it. The tab can wait.
